passage: Outside the mud house, the bullock cart was waiting to take everyone to the fair. Ojas sat on the step with his new canvas shoes. Trisha Didi bent down to help. "No!" He pushed her hand away. "I do it." He made one loop, lost it, made it again, tongue between his teeth. The cart driver coughed. Trisha waited. At last Ojas pulled a wobbly bow tight and jumped up, stamping. "See! Myself!" His grin stretched ear to ear. He did the second shoe too, slowly, and nobody said a word.

qa.q: What did Ojas push away?
qa.a: He pushed Trisha Didi's hand away.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel when he jumps up and stamps?
qa.a: He feels proud and excited, shown by his huge grin and his shout of 'See! Myself!'

qa.q: Which choice by Trisha Didi helped Ojas, and why?
qa.a: She waited even though the cart driver was impatient, which gave Ojas the time to succeed on his own and feel proud.

qa.q: What is it like for the cart driver to wait?
qa.a: The driver may feel impatient, which shows in the cough, but gets a family ready to go with a very happy little boy.

grounding: A young child refuses help with his laces and ties them himself, taking pride in doing it alone.

passage: Rain streaked the window of the Johannesburg flat, and the school bus was due in ten minutes. Zanele knelt with Alejandro's shoe. "Let me, love, we're late." Alejandro snatched his foot back and put both hands over the laces. "Mine. I can." Zanele took a breath and sat back on her heels. He crossed the laces, poked one under, pulled. It came undone. He tried again, frowning hard. The third time, the bow held. He looked up, eyes shining. "I did it by my own self!" Zanele laughed and kissed his hair. They ran for the bus together.

qa.q: How long was it until the school bus was due?
qa.a: The school bus was due in ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Alejandro cover the laces with both hands?
qa.a: He wanted to tie them himself and was determined not to be helped, even though they were late.

qa.q: What turning point let Alejandro try, and what did it give him?
qa.a: Zanele sat back on her heels instead of insisting, which let him succeed on the third try and feel proud of doing it by himself 🙂

qa.q: What is the morning like for Zanele?
qa.a: Zanele is worried about being late, but chooses to wait and ends up sharing his joy, laughing as they run for the bus.

grounding: A child insists on tying his own shoes despite a rush, and shows pride when he manages it.

passage: After yoga in the kindergarten hall, twenty children sat down to put their shoes back on. Kalyani, their teacher, crouched beside Ritu, whose laces were trailing. "Shall I?" Ritu shook her head hard and pushed the teacher's fingers off the lace. "Ritu will do it." It took a long time. The others lined up at the door. Ritu made a big floppy loop, then another, and twisted them together. It wasn't really a bow, but it stayed. She marched to the line with her chin up. "I tied it. Nobody helped." Kalyani wrote a note to herself: let Ritu try first.

qa.q: What did the children do after yoga?
qa.a: They sat down to put their shoes back on.

qa.q: What does Ritu marching with her chin up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud of tying the lace alone, even though it wasn't a perfect bow.

qa.q: What choice did Kalyani make for the future, and why is it helpful?
qa.a: Kalyani decided to let Ritu try first, which respects Ritu's wish for independence and builds her confidence.

qa.q: How might the children waiting in line see Ritu's slow tying?
qa.a: They might feel a bit impatient at the door, but they also see that a classmate can do something hard alone.

grounding: A kindergarten child pushes her teacher's hand away and ties her shoes herself, proud to do it alone.

I'm Kiran, Baljeet's big sister. I'm ten. Yesterday we went to buy his new school shoes. The shop uncle knelt down to tie the laces for him.
Baljeet pulled his foot back and pushed the uncle's hand away. "Me! I'm five!"
Everyone waited. He crossed the laces, made one loop, lost it, made it again. His tongue was poking out. It took forever. The bow was wobbly.
Then he stood up and stamped his feet and looked at all of us like he had won a race.

qa.a: The shop uncle.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he stamped his feet at the end?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased with himself, as if he had won a race, because he tied the laces on his own.

qa.a: They waited patiently even though it took a long time, which let Baljeet finish and feel proud.

qa.q: How might the shop uncle feel when Baljeet pushes his hand away?
qa.a: He might be a little surprised, then amused and happy to see a small boy so keen to do it himself.

grounding: It shows, through a sister's eyes, a young child pushing an adult's hand away from his laces and proudly tying them alone.

Monday. Mohit Chacha bent to tie Divyansh's shoes. Divyansh, five, pushed his hand away. "I do it!" He tried, and the laces flopped apart. He cried and kicked the shoe.

Saturday. Sports day. Divyansh tied both shoes before anyone could offer. The bows were lopsided. He ran to show Chacha, grinning. "Myself!"

passage:
In the courtyard of their village house near Mangalore, Chandrika, five, sat on the step with her new school shoes and their long, floppy laces.
Her grandfather Francis bent down. "Come, I'll tie them."
Chandrika pushed his hand away. "No! I do it myself!"
She made one loop. It fell apart. She tried again, tongue sticking out, while the bus horn sounded down the lane.
"Wait, Grandpa!"
The second loop held. A wobbly bow.
She stamped her foot to show him. "I did it!"
Francis laughed and clapped, and they ran for the bus together.

qa.q: What was Chandrika trying to tie?
qa.a: The laces of her new school shoes.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling when she stamped her foot and said "I did it!"?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased, having tied the laces by herself.

qa.q: How could Francis support Chandrika's wish to do things herself on busy mornings?
qa.a: He could give her a little extra time to try, and step in only if she asks, so she can keep building her independence.

qa.q: How might Francis feel about being pushed away?
qa.a: He might feel a little amused and proud, seeing her so determined to do it herself.

grounding: It shows a young child pushing an adult's hand away to tie her own laces, proud of doing it herself.

passage:
On a cold morning in Johannesburg, Thabo, five, stood at the door with his winter coat hanging open.
Zeynep, who minded him before school, reached for the zip. "Let me."
Thabo stepped back. "No! Me!"
He pinched the two ends together. They slipped. He tried again, frowning hard. Zeynep folded her arms and waited, though they were already late.
The third time, the zip caught. He pulled it up to his chin and looked at her, eyes shining.
"Myself," he said.
"Yourself," Zeynep agreed, and he marched to the car with his chest puffed out.

qa.q: Where did Thabo live?
qa.a: In Johannesburg.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he pulled the zip up to his chin?
qa.a: He felt proud and pleased, eyes shining at doing it himself.

qa.q: What did Zeynep do that helped Thabo?
qa.a: She waited patiently even though they were late, letting him try until he managed on his own.

qa.q: What was it like for Zeynep to wait?
qa.a: She may have felt a little impatient about being late, but she chose to let him have his moment.

grounding: It shows a young child refusing help with his zip and taking pride in doing it himself.

passage:
At the kindergarten, it was time for outdoor play, and Lalit, five, sat on the bench with one shoe untied.
Sunaina, the teacher, knelt. "I'll tie it quickly."
Lalit covered his shoe with both hands. "No, I'm doing it."
The others ran past to the swings. Lalit made a loop, and it fell. He tried again, and again.
Sunaina sat beside him. "Take your time."
On the fourth try, a knot held. Lalit held up his foot. "I did it by myself!"
"All by yourself," Sunaina said.
He ran to the swings, hopping with pride.

qa.q: On which try did Lalit's knot hold?
qa.a: A knot held on the fourth try.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he held up his foot?
qa.a: He felt proud and excited that he had done it by himself.

qa.q: Which choice by Sunaina helped, and why?
qa.a: Sitting beside him and saying "Take your time" helped, because it let him practise and feel pride in doing it himself.

qa.q: How might the children on the swings see Lalit?
qa.a: They might not notice, but Lalit feels bigger and prouder when he joins them.

grounding: It shows a young child refusing a teacher's help with his laces and taking pride in doing it himself.

passage:
First day of the summer holidays: Pallavi, five, pushed her mother Ira's hand off her sandal straps. "I do it!" She took ages. The strap was on the wrong hole. She wore it anyway.
Next week: Pallavi sat on the step with her new school shoes, tongue poking out, pulling at the laces. When Ira bent down, Pallavi turned her whole body away. "No. Me."
End of the holidays: Pallavi tied a wobbly bow all by herself. She ran through the flat holding up one foot. "Mumma! Look! Nobody helped!"
Ira clapped. Pallavi tied the other shoe too, even slower, beaming.

qa.q: Whose hand did Pallavi push off her sandal straps?
qa.a: She pushed her mother Ira's hand off.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when she tied the bow by herself?
qa.a: She felt very proud and excited, running through the flat to show that nobody helped.

qa.q: How could Ira keep supporting Pallavi's wish to do things alone?
qa.a: Keep giving her time to try, step in only when asked, and cheer her success as Ira did.

qa.q: What is it like for Ira when Pallavi turns away from her help?
qa.a: She may feel a little pushed aside, but also proud to see her daughter becoming independent.

grounding: Over a holiday, a child pushes her mother's hand away and learns to fasten and tie her own shoes, proud of doing it herself.

The Christmas service at the church in Aizawl would start in ten minutes, and the whole family was waiting at the door. Lalremsiami, five, sat on the floor with one shoe untied.
Her uncle Harish knelt to help. She pushed his hand away. "No! I can do it!"
"Mawii, we'll be late."
"I DO IT." She crossed the laces, missed, tried again. Her face went red.
Harish looked at his watch, then sat down on the step beside her. "Okay. Show me."
It took four tries. The bow was loose and crooked. Lalremsiami stood up, chin high. "I did it myself."
They ran to church and slipped in during the first carol.

qa.q: How many tries did it take Lalremsiami to tie the bow?
qa.a: It took four tries.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when she stood up with her chin high?
qa.a: She felt proud of herself for tying her shoe alone, even though the bow was loose and crooked.

qa.q: What did Harish do that helped, even though they were in a hurry?
qa.a: He sat beside her and said 'Show me', giving her the chance to do it herself instead of taking over.

qa.q: How might Harish feel waiting while the church service is about to start?
qa.a: He probably feels anxious about being late, but chooses patience because he sees how much it matters to her.

grounding: A child pushes her uncle's hand away from her laces and insists on tying them herself, proud of doing it alone.

It was the first cold morning of winter in Lucknow, and Asif's father held out his woollen cap and scarf. Asif, six, pulled back. "I can do it myself!"
He put the cap on backwards. He wound the scarf round and round until only his eyes showed.
His older brother Farhan laughed. "You look like a mummy."
Asif pulled the scarf lower and put his hands on his hips. "I chose it. I did it."
His father smiled and did not fix it. He only held out Asif's shoes. Asif sat down at once and started pulling the laces himself.

qa.q: What did Asif's father hold out to him first?
qa.a: His father held out his woollen cap and scarf.

qa.q: Why did Asif put his hands on his hips after Farhan laughed?
qa.a: He felt proud of choosing and doing it himself, and a little defensive when his brother teased him.

qa.q: What did Asif's father do well?
qa.a: He let Asif keep the cap and scarf his own way and handed him his shoes, giving him more chances to do things himself.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Asif's scarf?
qa.a: Farhan finds it funny, like a mummy, and does not see how proud Asif is.

grounding: A child pulls back from his father's help with his winter cap and scarf, proud to choose and do it himself.

Preschool note, Onam week

Today Jasleen, four, refused help with her new sandals' buckles. When I reached to fasten them, she pushed my hand away and said, 'I want to do it by myself.' When the buckle finally clicked, she beamed and showed everyone. I will let her have extra time at shoe-changing and praise her effort.

Anu, class teacher
